slides.title: Feature flags: the basic idea
slides.body:
Choose which existing application behavior runs, using configuration that can change after deployment.

We’ll explain the decision first, then see it in Sky’s recommendation and promo-rail examples.
slides.notes: Start on the slides, with the app closed or in another tab. Say: “Before we touch Amplitude, let’s agree on what a feature flag actually does. It is a named decision our application checks while it runs. We deploy the code that supports a change, then use configuration to decide when and for whom that change is released.” Give the room the shape of the session: concepts, a short demonstration, hands-on practice, then Sky’s architecture discussion.
slides.cut: Keep the explanation concrete; use the recommendation rail as the running example.

slides.title: Deploy code; choose when to release it
slides.body:
Deploy

Install the supported paths

The application contains the current behavior and the new behavior.

Release

Decide who uses the new path

A flag returns a value at runtime. The application acts on it.

Changing a flag updates a decision. Adding a new capability still requires application code.
slides.notes: Say: “Imagine we have built a new recommendation-ranking strategy. We can deploy it alongside the existing strategy while keeping everyone on the existing one. The flag lets us release the new strategy to a test audience, then expand that audience. Switching the flag off selects the existing strategy again.” Explain that a flag is not a remote code installer. Ask: “Could you deploy on Tuesday and release to viewers on Thursday?” Answer yes, provided both paths and the flag check are already deployed.
slides.cut: Keep the explanation concrete; use the recommendation rail as the running example.

slides.title: What can a flag control?
slides.body:
Backend

Recommendation behavior

Choose which ranking strategy or service path produces the rail.

Content presentation

Promo-rail composition

Choose a new collection, ordering or promotional treatment.

Client

The viewer interface

Choose which supported layout or component is rendered.

Application code defines the effect. Targeting rules define who receives it.
slides.notes: Walk through Sky’s backend use cases first. Say: “A flag doesn’t have to control a button. It can select an algorithm, an API implementation or how a content rail is assembled. The same idea works in a TV client or browser.” Keep the distinction between behavior and audience clear: code knows how to build the rail; the flag’s rules decide which users receive that behavior. Authoritative subscription checks remain in their normal systems; a demo flag is not a replacement for entitlement enforcement.
slides.cut: Keep the explanation concrete; use the recommendation rail as the running example.

slides.title: The parts of a feature flag
slides.body:
• KeyThe name application code asks for, such as recommendation-rail.
  • VariantsPossible results: on selects the new path; off selects the default in our app.
  • Targeting + rolloutRules for eligibility and allocation, such as high engagement at 100%.
  • User contextA stable identity and the properties needed to evaluate those rules.
slides.notes: Introduce the vocabulary before any SDK discussion. Say: “The key is a stable identifier, not necessarily the display name. A variant is the value we get back. Our app treats the literal on value as enabled. A targeting rule might select high-engagement viewers; allocation decides how many of those eligible viewers receive on.” Explain that percentage rollout is based on a bucketing identity and configuration rather than a fresh coin toss on each page load. Consistency depends on keeping the relevant identity, rules and bucketing settings aligned.
slides.cut: Keep the explanation concrete; use the recommendation rail as the running example.

slides.title: How a flag is evaluated
slides.body: Rules + user context → variant → application behavior. Casey’s low engagement would select the default path.
slides.notes: Trace the diagram left to right. Say: “The evaluator needs two inputs: the flag configuration and the viewer context. Here the rule targets high engagement, and Aroha’s engagement is high. The evaluator checks the rule and allocation, then returns on. Our application code interprets on and calls the new rail implementation.” Contrast Casey, who has low engagement and receives off under this rule. Say: “The returned value is data. Our code chooses what to do with it.” Then bridge to architecture: “Now we can ask where this evaluator lives, how it gets configuration, and which network requests are involved.” Do not open the app yet.
slides.cut: Keep the explanation concrete; use the recommendation rail as the running example.

slides.title: Configuration and evaluation are separate
slides.body:
Control planeCreate rules, variants and rollout
→
Delivery + SDKRetrieve configuration or decisions
→
ApplicationUse the result at the decision point

Source: Experiment quick start
slides.notes: A deployment groups flags delivered to a particular integration. In the workshop all participant flags join the web client deployment. A server deployment would belong to the backend service. A flag key and a management API flag ID are different identifiers.

slides.title: Local and remote evaluation
slides.body:
Local evaluationRemote evaluation
Decision happensInside the SDK runtimeAt Amplitude
Decision inputsLocally available user dataRequest data + supported enrichment
Network on decision pathNo, after configuration loadsYes, when fetching a decision

Server-side code can use either mode. Remote does not mean browser-only.

Source: Remote evaluation
slides.notes: Refer back to the evaluator box in the previous diagram. With local evaluation, that box sits inside the SDK runtime, which can be a backend service. With remote evaluation, that box sits at Amplitude and the caller fetches a result. Server-side code can use either mode. Explain that remote enrichment can use stored Analytics properties, while local evaluation needs the relevant inputs available locally or supported sync configuration. The static app will demonstrate remote evaluation; it does not benchmark a server SDK.

slides.title: Three operations, three timings
slides.body:
1

Fetch a decision

Network round trip plus service and SDK work.

2

Read a cached variant

Read an already fetched decision. No rule evaluation is implied.

3

Evaluate locally

Run rules against a user and cached configuration.

A quick cached read does not measure remote evaluation latency.
slides.notes: Explain the three operations using the slide before opening the app. A remote fetch includes network and SDK work. A variant read retrieves a result already stored by the client. A local evaluation executes targeting logic against available user data and downloaded configuration. We will observe fetch and cached-read timings in the app later; neither is a benchmark of Sky backend local evaluation.

slides.title: Caches have different jobs
slides.body:
SDK

Stored decisions

Used by variant reads until the app fetches again.

Delivery

CDN cache

Amortises remote requests. Flag changes invalidate deployment caches.

Local SDK

Flag configuration

Refresh rules separately from request-time evaluation.

A changed rule still needs to reach the application. Test the whole rollback path.

Source: Performance and caching
slides.notes: Explain that browser cached reads are different from CDN response caches. Do not promise instantaneous rollback everywhere. In this app the attendee must click Evaluate flags after editing a remote flag. Polling, startup and refresh behavior depend on the chosen SDK and integration.

slides.title: Design latency and failure behavior
slides.body:
1. Choose a refresh strategy and a time budget.
  2. Serve an intentional default when evaluation is unavailable.
  3. Measure from Sky’s actual runtime and network location.
Done when: there is an owner for defaults and refresh behavior

Seed historical profiles before the session. Property enrichment can lag profile updates.
slides.notes: For recommendation services, ask if a default rail is acceptable during an outage. This app discards the prior identity’s decision and shows the default during a fetch or on failure. Other production systems may choose last-known-good for the same identity; that is an explicit engineering choice.

slides.title: Rollout and rollback need observation
slides.body:
ReleaseStart with QA or an eligible segment
→
RampIncrease allocation; watch guardrails
→
RollbackDisable, refresh, verify the default

Track errors, rail load time and engagement alongside the rollout.
slides.notes: Discuss a staged 1%, 10%, 50%, 100% release as an example, not an automatic policy. Verify consistent identities. Reducing allocation and disabling a flag are different actions. A flag controls the new path; it is not content authorisation.

slides.title: Flags and experiments share delivery
slides.body:
Feature flag

Who receives a release?

Targeting, variants, assignment and rollout controls.

Experiment

What effect did it have?

A hypothesis, exposure measurement, success metrics and analysis.

Source: Data model
slides.notes: A release can use the same delivery concepts as an experiment. Turning on a flag does not establish causal impact. For a rail experiment, define exposure at the point the rail is encountered and measure a decision metric such as playback starts with guardrails.

slides.title: Manage configuration programmatically
slides.body:
GET   /api/1/flags?projectId=896821
POST  /api/1/flags
PATCH /api/1/flags/{flagId}
      {"enabled": false}

Management API: configuration changes.
SDK / evaluation API: runtime decisions.

Presenter examples use management credentials outside the static site.

Source: Management API flag endpoints
slides.notes: Open api-examples.html. Walk through a list, create and disable call. The create example associates a flag with a deployment but leaves activation to an explicit step. Management API access requires a separate management key, not either browser key. Runtime REST examples require a server deployment key. No participant runs these privileged calls.
slides.cut: Cut point: show the list and disable calls only; the full examples remain in the guide.

slides.title: See the decision in the streaming app
slides.body:
1. Use the live presenter-recommendations flag.
  2. Evaluate Aroha: high engagement selects the new rail.
  3. Evaluate Casey: low engagement selects the default rail.

Same application code; different viewer context; different result.

Open workshop hub ↗
slides.notes: This is the first app demonstration, after 25 minutes of explanation. Open the live presenter scenario with explicit properties and the high-engagement rule active. Evaluate Aroha, then select Casey and wait for automatic evaluation. Connect each observed result to the evaluator diagram. Keep this to two minutes so participants have time to open their own workspaces. Save the identity-only demonstration and rollback for the relevant stations; the separate app-demo script provides the longer spoken walkthrough.
slides.cut: Show Aroha and Casey only; move to participant setup at minute 27.

slides.title: Open your workshop workspace
slides.body:
1. Open the app and exercise guide from the hub.
  2. Select Live once the presenter has configured the deployment.
  3. Choose a unique prefix: alex-recommendations.
  4. Use project Feature Flag workshop and the shared web client deployment.
Done when: you can find the project, app and viewer selector
Open workshop hub ↗
slides.notes: After the presenter demonstration, ask participants to open the app and exercise guide. Confirm the Feature Flag workshop project and permissions. Each attendee uses their own unique flag prefix. Have a presenter flag ready for anyone without edit access. Practice mode is explicitly a simulation; use Live when connected.

slides.title: 1 / Create your recommendation flag
slides.body:
1. Create a remote-evaluation flag with your unique key and an on variant.
  2. Attach the workshop web deployment and activate at 100%.
  3. Paste the key into the app and evaluate.
  4. Target subscription_packages containing Sky Sport; leave other users off.
  5. Compare Aroha, Ben and Dev.
Done when: Aroha and Dev see the new rail; Ben sees the default

Use identity + profile properties for this station. Incognito alone does not change identity.

Open workshop hub ↗
slides.notes: At minute 30 begin this station. Confirm all-other-users is off; the target segment allocates 100% to on. With array properties use the available contains/member operator for Sky Sport and check the UI preview. Aroha and Dev qualify. Ben does not. The app treats only the literal variant value on as enabled. If anyone is stuck, pair them with a working participant or use the presenter flag.

slides.title: 2 / Test identity and release scope
slides.body:
1. Remove the subscription rule; set an all-user rollout to 50%.
  2. Compare all five viewers, then re-evaluate the same viewer.
  3. Copy the scenario URL into Incognito; keep the identity unchanged.
  4. Switch the selected viewer to test another identity.
  5. Disable the flag in Amplitude and evaluate again.
Done when: the new rail disappears after rollback and refresh

Five viewers may not split evenly at 50%. Flag keys are in the URL; connection keys are not.
slides.notes: By minute 42 move to percentage rollout. Keep consistent bucketing settings. Incognito may need keys entered again until they are deployed in config.js. Same identity is necessary for stable comparison; other rule inputs and configuration must stay the same too. Do not imply a five-user sample must split 2/3. Confirm the real rollback in Amplitude and fetch again. Practice rollback is available only in simulated mode.

slides.title: 3 / Use what Amplitude knows
slides.body:
1. Set engagement_level = high as the target at 100%; everyone else off.
  2. Select “Send identity only” and evaluate Aroha and Casey.
  3. Expand Request inputs: no profile properties are sent.
  4. Inspect the seeded user profiles in Amplitude.
  5. Explain where the request and the enrichment happen.
Done when: Aroha qualifies, Casey does not, with identity-only requests

The fixture panel shows expected data. Inspect Amplitude to verify the stored profile.
slides.notes: Start at minute 52 and finish by 65. Ensure previous rules are removed. In the live rehearsal verify Aroha high and Casey low ahead of time. The server enriches the remote request from stored Analytics properties. The browser inspector cannot show Amplitude’s private enrichment internals; use profile inspection plus identity-only requests and outcomes as evidence. Property freshness can lag, so do not make attendees update a profile and expect an immediate change. If profiles are not ready, demonstrate explicit inputs and explain why this station cannot yet be verified.

slides.title: Now / map the current decision path
slides.body:
TV / streaming clientWhere is the rail requested?
→
Sky backendWhere is the behavior selected?
→
User dataWhich system owns each input?

Map one recommendation or promo request together.
slides.notes: We do not yet know Sky’s current architecture. Ask the room to draw clients, API gateway, recommendation service, cache and user data sources. Find the decision point, current release mechanism, acceptable default, latency budget and the team that owns it. Record facts separately from proposals.
slides.cut: Cut point: map one backend service only.

slides.title: Next / introduce one backend flag
slides.body:
Decision point

Recommendation service

Choose one behavior with an owned default and rollback path.

Evaluation mode

Choose per requirement

Local for available inputs; remote when enrichment is needed.

Verification

Observe the result

Measure latency, error rate, exposure and user experience.

This is a proposal for discussion. The workshop app does not run a backend.
slides.notes: Discuss a first flag around a backend rail selector. Compare supplying trusted subscription facts to a local SDK against requesting remote enrichment for an engagement-driven change. Subscription entitlements still need authoritative enforcement. The app’s editable viewer is a teaching fixture, not an authentication model.

slides.title: Future / consistent delivery across platforms
slides.body:
SDKs

Shared evaluation contracts

Identity, defaults, variant types and refresh behavior.

Operations

Owned flag lifecycles

Permissions, CI integration, expiry and cleanup.

Measurement

Connect release to outcomes

Intentional exposure, guardrails and experiments.

Cross-platform consistency needs aligned identity, rules and bucketing; it is not automatic.
slides.notes: Ask what would make this ideal for Sky’s TV platforms and backend teams. SDKs package lifecycle, caching, evaluation and integration behavior, reducing custom plumbing. Verify support for each target language and TV runtime before choosing an implementation. Capture next actions and owners rather than asserting a future architecture.
slides.cut: Cut point: collect one desired outcome and one owner from the room.

slides.title: Wave / standard demonstration
slides.body:
Simon’s standard Wave demo.

Connect the demonstration to a question raised during the workshop, then return for questions.
slides.notes: Switch to your standard Wave environment and run your usual demonstration. No custom Wave setup is included in this pack. Keep the eight-minute limit and return to the closing slide.

slides.title: Questions and next steps
slides.body:
1. Which backend decision is the first candidate?
  2. Which evaluation mode fits its data and latency needs?
  3. Who owns setup, verification and the rollback rehearsal?
Done when: there is a concrete next step
Open workshop hub ↗

Optional buffer station: create a second promo flag and copy a scenario containing both keys.
slides.notes: Use this time for questions and recovery. Optional station 4 is the promo flag: create a second remote on/off flag, attach the same deployment, enter its key, target Movies and compare Ben with Aroha. This is extra practice, not a prerequisite. End by capturing the owner of the first technical follow-up.
slides.cut: Optional station 4 is the first material to omit if time is tight.
